query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex high-entropy alloys that start as a single-phase material, the combination of service-temperature thermal activation and cyclic mechanical loading leads to localized atomic ordering at grain boundaries. This ordering facilitates the nucleation of incipient brittle intermetallic phases that degrade toughness. The mechanism is distinct from conventional alloys where grain-boundary segregation or rapid, extensive intermetallic precipitation dominates.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy alloy with compositionally complex, uniformly distributed elements.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal exposure (at moderate service temperatures) combined with cyclic mechanical loading to promote diffusion and ordering.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant temperatures and cyclic loading conditions that mimic long-term usage without reaching extremes that would induce complete phase transformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized atomic ordering at grain boundaries that acts as nucleation sites for brittle intermetallic phases.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained thermal and mechanical stress, local diffusion kinetics at the grain boundaries are enhanced. This leads to incipient ordering in these regions, which serves as a precursor for the formation of brittle intermetallic phases. These phases create weak spots that are responsible for the observed degradation in toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the thermomechanically treated alloy will exhibit a measurable drop in toughness (e.g., lower fracture toughness values), with microstructural analysis revealing early-stage intermetallic precipitation or ordered domains localized at grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: The as-processed single-phase high-entropy alloy, featureless with respect to grain-boundary segregation or precipitate formation, and with favorable strength–ductility characteristics.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under moderate service-temperature conditions with cyclic loading. At very high temperatures or under extreme mechanical conditions that cause complete phase transformations, different mechanisms may predominate.
generation.uncertainty: The specific kinetics and extent of atomic ordering, as well as the precise decrease in toughness, remain uncertain and will likely depend on the detailed alloy composition and the exact service conditions imposed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the high-entropy alloy in the as-processed state and subject them to a controlled thermal aging and cyclic loading protocol that simulates long-term service conditions. A baseline set of samples should be maintained without treatment. After treatment, perform fracture toughness testing alongside detailed microstructural analyses using high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM, SEM coupled with EDS) to detect any local ordering or onset of intermetallic formation at grain boundaries.
measurements: Fracture toughness (K_IC) comparison between treated and baseline samples
Quantitative microstructural imaging to identify local ordering or intermetallic precipitates
Elemental distribution analysis at grain boundaries to assess segregation or ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the treated samples show no significant drop in toughness compared to the baseline, and if microstructural analyses do not reveal any evidence of localized atomic ordering or incipient intermetallic phase formation at grain boundaries under the applied service conditions.
